'''Daniel Mertz Kane''' (born 1986) is an American mathematician. He is a full professor with a joint position in the Mathematics Department and the Computer Science and Engineering Department at the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name="nfw">{{citation|title=New Faculty Watch: George Porter, Daniel M. Kane|publisher=UC San Diego Computer Science and Engineering|url=http://cse.ucsd.edu/node/2534|access-date=2015-01-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115104850/http://cse.ucsd.edu/node/2534|archive-date=2015-01-15|url-status=dead}}.</ref>

==Early life and education==
Kane was born in [[Madison, Wisconsin]], to [[Janet E. Mertz]] and Jonathan M. Kane, professors of [[oncology]] and of mathematics and computer science, respectively.<ref name="morgan">{{citation|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200704/comm-morgan-web.pdf|title=2007 Morgan Prize|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|volume=54|issue=4|pages=521–522|date=April 2007}}.</ref><ref name="nyt">{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/10/education/10math.html?pagewanted=all|title=Math Skills Suffer in U.S., Study Finds|first=Sara|last=Rimer|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 10, 2008}}. The article is primarily about a study jointly authored by Kane's parents, but also mentions Kane's IMO results.</ref>

He attended Wingra School, a small alternative K-8 school in Madison that focuses on [[autodidactism|self-guided education]]. By 3rd grade, he had mastered K through 9th-grade mathematics.<ref name="morgan"/> Starting at age 13, he took honors math courses at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] and did research under the mentorship of [[Ken Ono]] while dual enrolled at [[Madison West High School]].<ref>{{citation|title=Madison grad described as genius mathematician |url=http://www.math.wisc.edu/~ono/kane3.html |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |date=August 6, 2003 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060829062539/http://www.math.wisc.edu/~ono/kane3.html |archive-date=2006-08-29 }}.</ref> He earned gold medals in the 2002 and 2003 [[International Mathematical Olympiad]]s.<ref name="nyt"/><ref>{{IMO results |id=6904 |name=Daniel Kane}}</ref>  Prior to his 17th birthday, he resolved an open conjecture proposed years earlier by [[George Andrews (mathematician)|Andrews]] and Lewis; for this research, he was named Fellow Laureate of the [[Davidson Institute for Talent Development]].<ref>[http://www.davidsongifted.org/fellows/Article/Davidson_Fellows___2003_343.aspx 2003 Davidson Fellow Laureates] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115105119/http://www.davidsongifted.org/fellows/Article/Davidson_Fellows___2003_343.aspx |date=2015-01-15 }}, Davidson Institute, accessed 2015-01-14.</ref>

He graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 2007 with two bachelor's degrees, one in mathematics with computer science and the other in physics.<ref name="nfw"/>
While at MIT, Kane was one of four people since 2003 (and one of nine in the history of the competition) to be named a four-time Putnam Fellow in the [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition]].<ref>Joseph A. Gallian, [http://www.d.umn.edu/~jgallian/putnam.pdf The Putnam Competition from 1938-2012].</ref> He also won the 2007 [[Morgan Prize]]<ref name="morgan"/> and competed as part of the MIT team in the [[Mathematical Contest in Modeling]] four times, earning the highest score three times and winning the Ben Fusaro Award in 2004, INFORMS Award in 2006, and [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] Award in 2007.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.siam.org/news/news.php?id=1136|journal=SIAM News|publisher=[[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]]|date=June 12, 2007|first=Michelle|last=Sipics|title=MIT's "Dream Team" Wins SIAM Award for MCM 07}}.</ref> He also won the [[Machtey Award]] as an undergraduate in 2005, with Tim Abbott and Paul Valiant, for the best student-authored
paper at the [[Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science]] that year, on the complexity of two-player win-loss games.<ref>[https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~FOCS05/program.pdf FOCS 2005 program], retrieved 2015-01-15.</ref>

Kane received his doctorate in mathematics from [[Harvard University]] in 2011; his dissertation, on [[number theory]], was supervised by [[Barry Mazur]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=159319}}</ref> In his [[curriculum vitae]], Kane lists as mentors [[Ken Ono]] while in high school; [[Erik Demaine]], [[Joseph Gallian]], and Cesar Silva while an undergraduate student at MIT; and [[Barry Mazur]], [[Benedict Gross]], and Henry Cohn while a graduate student at Harvard.<ref>[http://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~dakane/cv.pdf Curriculum vitae], retrieved 2015-01-15.</ref>

==Research contributions==
In 2010, joint work with [[Jelani Nelson]] and [[David P. Woodruff|David Woodruff]] won both the IBM Pat Goldberg Memorial<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://researcher.watson.ibm.com/researcher/view_group_subpage.php?id=2528 |title=IBM Pat Goldberg Memorial Best Paper Award |access-date=2015-01-31 |archive-date=2023-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230421133917/https://researcher.watson.ibm.com/researcher/view_group_subpage.php?id=2528 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and [[Symposium on Principles of Database Systems]] (PODS) best paper awards<ref>[http://www.sigmod2010.org/program_pods.shtml PODS 2010 program], accessed 2015-01-14;</ref> for work on an optimal algorithm for the [[count-distinct problem]].

The bulk of his modern research consists of computational statistics, with a focus in [[robust statistics]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Introductory Papers|url=https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~dakane/IntroductoryPapers.html|website=cseweb.ucsd.edu|access-date=2025-12-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Daniel Kane's Homepage|url=https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~dakane/|website=cseweb.ucsd.edu|access-date=2025-12-02}}</ref>
